the resistance of dairy cows to electric current is variable, that the behavioral response to electric current is dependent upon the pathway through the cow and that cows are more sensitive to shocks through the mouth-all hooved pathway than to those through the front-rear hooved pathway.
the mouth-all hoofs pathway is the most sensitive pathway in dairy cows, and that the mouth-all hoof pathway is more sensitive than the front-rear hoof pathway.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model for predicting animal sensitivity to electrical current based on the electrical resistance of pathways through the animal.
the development and use of a behavioral methodology to assess the sensitivity of dairy cattle to electrical shocks.
the development of a method for assessing the relative sensitivity of individual animals to electrical current.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dairy cattle are sensitive to electrical currents, and that the pathways through which the current is conducted and the magnitude of the current determine the degree of sensitivity.

the electrical resistance of a cow is a function of the pathway through the animal, the electrical conductivity of the pathway tissues, and the electrical conductivity of any insulating materials present.
dairy cattle have an aversion to electrical shock, but that the magnitude of the aversion is dependent on the pathway of the shock.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dairy cattle can be sensitized to electrical currents, and that a specific avoidance response can be conditioned for a mouth-all-hooves shock.
the front-rear hooved pathway was the least sensitive, followed by the mouth-rear hooved and the front-all hooved pathways.
a front-rear hoof shock of 3.0mA is the most appropriate level for the application of electric shock to dairy cattle.

the resistance of a dairy cow to an electric fence varies significantly between cows, and between pathways through an individual cow.
